name: Metaphor
definition: Describing one thing as if it were another, without “like” or “as”, so that the qualities of the second carry over to the first.
example: All the world’s a stage, / And all the men and women merely players.
source: William Shakespeare, As You Like It

name: Simile
definition: An open comparison between two unlike things, usually made with “like” or “as”.
example: I wandered lonely as a cloud

name: Extended metaphor
definition: A single metaphor carried through several lines, a whole poem or a long passage, developed point by point.
example: Shakespeare’s “All the world’s a stage” speech keeps the comparison going through the seven ages of a life, each one a role played on the same stage.

name: Conceit
definition: An ingenious, often surprising comparison between two very different things, worked out at length. The metaphysical poets made it their signature.
example: In “A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning”, John Donne compares two parted lovers to the two legs of a drawing compass: one stays fixed while the other travels, and they stay joined.

name: Analogy
definition: A comparison that explains something unfamiliar by setting out how it works like something familiar. It argues as well as decorates.
example: Memory is less a filing cabinet than a riverbed: what is stored there is always being reshaped by what flows through.

name: Symbolism
definition: Using an object, person or event to stand for an idea larger than itself, so that it carries meaning beyond its literal place in the story.
example: The scarlet letter that Hester Prynne must wear in Hawthorne’s novel stands for shame at first, and gradually for something closer to strength.

name: Allegory
definition: A whole story in which characters, places and events stand for ideas, so that it can be read on a second, usually moral or political, level.
example: In John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, a man called Christian travels through the Slough of Despond and Vanity Fair on his way to the Celestial City.

name: Personification
definition: Giving human feelings, actions or speech to something that is not human: an object, an animal, an idea or a force of nature.
example: Because I could not stop for Death – / He kindly stopped for me –

name: Anthropomorphism
definition: Presenting animals, gods or objects as actually behaving like people: talking, dressing, reasoning. It goes further than personification, which is a figure of speech.
example: In The Wind in the Willows, Mole, Rat and Toad keep houses, row boats and argue over lunch.

name: Zoomorphism
definition: Describing people, or things, with the qualities of animals.
example: He wolfed down his dinner and slunk off to bed, growling at anyone who spoke to him.

name: Hyperbole
definition: Deliberate, obvious exaggeration, used for emphasis, feeling or comedy rather than to be believed.
example: Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?

name: Litotes
definition: Understatement that affirms something by denying its opposite.
example: It was not the worst meal I have ever eaten (meaning: it was rather good).

name: Understatement
definition: Presenting something as smaller, milder or less important than it really is, often for irony or dry humour.
example: Mercutio, fatally wounded, calls his injury “a scratch, a scratch”.

name: Paradox
definition: A statement that seems to contradict itself but turns out, on reflection, to hold a truth.
example: I must be cruel only to be kind.

name: Oxymoron
definition: Two contradictory words placed side by side to create a compressed, striking effect.
example: O brawling love! O loving hate! … / Feather of lead, bright smoke, cold fire, sick health!

name: Idiom
definition: A fixed expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from its individual words.
example: “Break a leg”, “spill the beans”, “under the weather”.

name: Euphemism
definition: A mild or indirect word used in place of one that seems too blunt, harsh or embarrassing.
example: Saying someone has “passed away” rather than “died”, or that a company is “letting people go” rather than firing them.

name: Dysphemism
definition: The opposite of a euphemism: a deliberately harsh or crude word used in place of a neutral one.
example: Calling a car a “death trap”, or a doctor a “sawbones”.

name: Metonymy
definition: Referring to something by the name of a thing closely associated with it.
example: The pen is mightier than the sword (writing is more powerful than military force).

name: Synecdoche
definition: Using a part to stand for the whole, or the whole for a part.
example: “All hands on deck” (hands for sailors); “England won the match” (the country for its team).

name: Kenning
definition: A compound phrase that names something by describing it, common in Old English and Norse poetry.
example: “Whale-road” for the sea, “bone-house” for the body, as in Beowulf.

name: Circumlocution
definition: Talking around a subject in many words instead of naming it directly, whether to be tactful, evasive or comic.
example: Dickens’s Circumlocution Office in Little Dorrit exists to perfect the art of “how not to do it”.

name: Periphrasis
definition: Replacing a simple word with a longer descriptive phrase, often for elevation or variety.
example: Calling birds “the feathered tribe”, or the sun “the lamp of day”.

name: Transferred epithet
definition: An adjective moved from the person it describes to a thing connected with them. Also called hypallage.
example: He spent a sleepless night (it is the man, not the night, who does not sleep).

name: Epithet
definition: A descriptive word or phrase attached to a name that becomes almost part of it.
example: Homer’s “rosy-fingered Dawn”, “swift-footed Achilles”, “the wine-dark sea”.

name: Apostrophe
definition: Addressing someone absent or dead, or something not human, as if it could hear and answer.
example: Death, be not proud, though some have called thee / Mighty and dreadful

name: Allusion
definition: A brief, unexplained reference to a person, place, event or text the reader is expected to recognise.
example: Calling a tempting offer “a poisoned apple”, or a long journey home “an odyssey”.

name: Imagery
definition: Language that appeals to the senses (sight, sound, smell, taste, touch) so that the reader experiences a scene rather than being told about it.
example: The apparition of these faces in the crowd; / Petals on a wet, black bough.
source: Ezra Pound, “In a Station of the Metro”

name: Motif
definition: An image, object, phrase or idea that recurs through a work and gathers meaning with each return.
example: Blood in Macbeth: on daggers, on hands, in Lady Macbeth’s sleepwalking, always growing harder to wash away.

name: Pathetic fallacy
definition: Giving human emotions to nature or the weather, usually so the setting mirrors the mood of the characters.
example: A storm breaks over the moor on the night Heathcliff leaves Wuthering Heights.

name: Synesthesia
definition: Describing one sense in terms of another: a sound that has a colour, a colour that has a taste.
example: a loud shirt; a sweet melody; a velvety voice; a bitter wind

name: Antithesis
definition: Setting opposed ideas against each other in balanced, parallel phrases, so that each sharpens the other.
example: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times
source: Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities

name: Juxtaposition
definition: Placing two things side by side, without comment, so that the contrast or connection between them makes its own point.
example: A banquet scene cut straight against a beggar shivering outside the palace gate.

name: Anastrophe
definition: Inverting the normal order of words, for emphasis, rhythm or rhyme. Also called inversion.
example: Whose woods these are I think I know.
source: Robert Frost, “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening”

name: Connotation
definition: The feelings and associations a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning.
example: “Home” and “house” can name the same building, but only one suggests warmth and belonging.

name: Denotation
definition: The literal, dictionary meaning of a word, apart from the feelings it may suggest.
example: The denotation of “snake” is a legless reptile; its connotations may include danger and betrayal.

name: Zeugma
definition: One word, usually a verb, governing two others in different senses at once, often for wit.
example: Or stain her honour, or her new brocade
source: Alexander Pope, The Rape of the Lock

name: Pun
definition: Play on words that exploits a word with two meanings, or two words that sound alike.
example: Ask for me tomorrow, and you shall find me a grave man.
source: William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet (Mercutio, dying)

name: Bathos
definition: A sudden, unintended or comic drop from the elevated to the trivial.
example: He gave his life for his country, his family and his collection of spoons.

name: Pathos
definition: The quality in writing that stirs pity, sorrow or tenderness in the reader.
example: The death of Little Nell in Dickens’s The Old Curiosity Shop was written to move readers to tears, and it did.

name: Aphorism
definition: A short, memorable statement of a general truth or opinion.
example: Reading maketh a full man; conference a ready man; and writing an exact man.

name: Rhetorical question
definition: A question asked for effect, to make a point, with no answer expected.
example: If you prick us, do we not bleed?
source: William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice

name: Hypophora
definition: Raising a question and then answering it yourself, to guide the reader’s thinking.
example: What, then, is the purpose of a library? It is to keep the conversation of the dead open to the living.

name: Syllogism
definition: An argument in which a conclusion follows from two premises. Writers use it straight, or twist it for comedy.
example: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore Socrates is mortal.

name: Anachronism
definition: Something placed in a time where it does not belong, whether by mistake or on purpose for effect.
example: A clock strikes in Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar, set in ancient Rome, centuries before striking clocks existed.

name: Ubi sunt
definition: Latin for “where are they?”: a lament that asks where the people and glories of the past have gone.
example: But where are the snows of yester-year?
source: François Villon, trans. Dante Gabriel Rossetti

name: Verisimilitude
definition: The appearance of truth or reality in fiction, built from convincing detail, so that the reader believes in the world of the story.
example: Defoe gives Robinson Crusoe lists of salvaged tools, daily journal entries and careful accounts, so the island feels documented rather than invented.

name: Alliteration
definition: Repeating the same consonant sound at the start of words close together.
example: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.

name: Assonance
definition: Repeating the same vowel sound in nearby words, even when the consonants around it differ.
example: Hear the mellow wedding bells

name: Consonance
definition: Repeating consonant sounds within or at the end of nearby words, not only at the start.
example: pitter-patter; “And all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil”, from Hopkins’s “God’s Grandeur”.

name: Onomatopoeia
definition: A word that imitates the sound it names.
example: buzz, hiss, crackle, thud, murmur

name: Euphony
definition: A pleasing, smooth combination of sounds, often from soft consonants and long vowels.
example: Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness

name: Cacophony
definition: A harsh, jarring mix of sounds, often from hard consonants, used to suggest violence, disorder or ugliness.
example: The Jabberwock, “with eyes of flame, / Came whiffling through the tulgey wood, / And burbled as it came!”, from Lewis Carroll.

name: Sibilance
definition: Repeated hissing “s”, “sh” and soft “c” sounds, which can suggest whispering, the sea or menace.
example: And the silken, sad, uncertain rustling of each purple curtain

name: Internal rhyme
definition: A rhyme within a single line, rather than only at the ends of lines.
example: Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary

name: End rhyme
definition: Rhyme that falls on the last words of lines, the most familiar kind of rhyme in poetry.
example: Tyger Tyger, burning bright, / In the forests of the night

name: Slant rhyme
definition: An imperfect rhyme in which sounds are close but not identical. Also called half rhyme or near rhyme.
example: Emily Dickinson often pairs words like “soul” and “all”, or “room” and “storm”.

name: Eye rhyme
definition: Words that look as if they rhyme because they are spelled alike, but are pronounced differently.
example: love / move; cough / bough; heard / beard

name: Rhythm
definition: The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in language, the beat a reader feels in prose or verse.
example: The steady gallop of “I sprang to the stirrup, and Joris, and he” imitates riders at speed (Robert Browning).

name: Meter
definition: A regular, countable pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of verse.
example: Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day? — ten syllables of iambic pentameter: da-DUM five times.

name: Cadence
definition: The rise and fall of a voice in a sentence, especially the way a phrase comes to rest at its end.
example: The King James Bible is famous for its cadences: “And God said, Let there be light: and there was light.”

name: Refrain
definition: A line or phrase repeated at intervals in a poem or song, usually at the end of a stanza.
example: “Quoth the Raven, ‘Nevermore.’” closes stanza after stanza of Poe’s poem.

name: Caesura
definition: A pause or break in the middle of a line of verse, often marked by punctuation.
example: To err is human; to forgive, divine.
source: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism

name: Homophone
definition: Words that sound the same but differ in meaning or spelling, a favourite raw material for puns.
example: right / write / rite; sun / son

name: Anagram
definition: A word or phrase made by rearranging the letters of another.
example: “listen” and “silent”; Samuel Butler’s novel Erewhon spells “nowhere” almost backwards.

name: Palindrome
definition: A word, phrase or sentence that reads the same backwards as forwards.
example: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama.

name: Portmanteau
definition: A new word made by blending the sounds and meanings of two others.
example: Lewis Carroll’s “slithy” (lithe and slimy) and “chortle” (chuckle and snort).

name: Neologism
definition: A newly coined word or expression, or an old word given a new meaning.
example: Shakespeare is credited with the first recorded uses of “bedroom”, “lonely” and “eyeball”.

name: Malapropism
definition: The comic misuse of a word in place of a similar-sounding one.
example: Mrs Malaprop, in Sheridan’s The Rivals, calls someone “the very pineapple of politeness” (pinnacle).

name: Anaphora
definition: Repeating the same word or phrase at the start of successive clauses or lines.
example: In every cry of every Man, / In every Infants cry of fear

name: Epistrophe
definition: Repeating the same word or phrase at the end of successive clauses or lines.
example: government of the people, by the people, for the people

name: Anadiplosis
definition: Starting a clause with the word or phrase that ended the one before, building a chain.
example: tribulation worketh patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope

name: Epizeuxis
definition: Repeating a word immediately, with nothing in between, for intensity.
example: Words, words, words.

name: Diacope
definition: Repeating a word or phrase with one or a few words in between.
example: To be, or not to be

name: Polysyndeton
definition: Using more conjunctions than needed (“and … and … and”) to slow the pace or pile up effect.
example: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house

name: Asyndeton
definition: Leaving out the conjunctions between words or clauses, for speed and force.
example: Veni, vidi, vici — I came, I saw, I conquered.

name: Parallelism
definition: Giving related ideas the same grammatical structure, so that the form itself shows they belong together.
example: Some books are to be tasted, others to be swallowed, and some few to be chewed and digested

name: Isocolon
definition: A run of phrases of the same length and structure, a strict kind of parallelism.
example: Veni, vidi, vici: three verbs, two syllables each, the same shape.

name: Chiasmus
definition: Reversing the structure of a phrase in the next one, so the two mirror each other (A–B, B–A).
example: Fair is foul, and foul is fair

name: Antimetabole
definition: A kind of chiasmus that repeats the same words in reverse order.
example: Eat to live, and not live to eat.

name: Polyptoton
definition: Repeating a word in different grammatical forms within a sentence.
example: Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds

name: Tricolon
definition: A series of three parallel words, phrases or clauses, the “rule of three” that makes lists feel complete.
example: Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears

name: Climax
definition: As a figure of speech: arranging words or ideas in order of rising importance. (In plot, the word means the turning point of highest tension.)
example: Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon ’em.

name: Anticlimax
definition: A list or build-up that ends on something unexpectedly trivial, usually for comic effect.
example: Here thou, great Anna! whom three realms obey, / Dost sometimes counsel take — and sometimes tea.
source: Alexander Pope, The Rape of the Lock

name: Incremental repetition
definition: Repeating a line or stanza with a small change each time, so the story advances through the variations. Common in ballads.
example: In the ballad “Lord Randal”, the mother asks the same questions stanza by stanza, and each answer brings the poisoning closer to light.

name: Enumeration
definition: Listing the parts, causes or details of a subject one by one.
example: Whitman’s catalogues in “Song of Myself” enumerate carpenters, pilots, spinning-girls and farmers until the list becomes a nation.

name: Accumulation
definition: Piling up words or phrases that say similar things, to build pressure or sum up an argument.
example: He was a liar, a cheat, a schemer, a fraud from first to last.

name: Amplification
definition: Repeating a word or idea and adding detail to it, to stress and expand what might otherwise pass unnoticed.
example: It was a cold night — cold enough to freeze the ink in the well and the breath on the glass.

name: Tautology
definition: Saying the same thing twice in different words, often as a fault, sometimes for emphasis.
example: “free gift”, “new innovation”, “at this moment in time”.

name: Pleonasm
definition: Using more words than are needed to express an idea, sometimes clumsily, sometimes for emphasis.
example: “I saw it with my own eyes.”

name: Ellipsis
definition: Leaving out words that the reader can supply, or trailing off into silence (often marked with three dots).
example: Some people prefer tea; others, coffee (the verb “prefer” is understood the second time).

name: Foreshadowing
definition: Hints early in a story of what is to come, which prepare the reader and build suspense.
example: Romeo, before the party, fears “some consequence yet hanging in the stars” that will end in “untimely death”.

name: Flashback
definition: A scene that interrupts the present action to show events from earlier.
example: Wuthering Heights is told mostly as a long look back, as Nelly Dean recalls the history of the two families.

name: Flashforward
definition: A scene that jumps ahead to show what will happen later, before the story returns to the present.
example: In A Christmas Carol, the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come shows Scrooge his own neglected grave.

name: In medias res
definition: Latin for “into the middle of things”: beginning a story in the midst of the action, filling in the background later.
example: The Odyssey opens with Odysseus already stranded, ten years after Troy; his earlier wanderings are told later.

name: Frame story
definition: A story that contains other stories, often told by characters within it.
example: In The Canterbury Tales, pilgrims riding to Canterbury tell one another tales to pass the time.

name: Nonlinear narrative
definition: Telling events out of chronological order, so that meaning comes from how the pieces are arranged.
example: Emily Brontë moves back and forth across thirty years in Wuthering Heights, so the reader learns the past and the present in pieces.

name: Circular narrative
definition: A story that ends where it began, in the same place, situation or words, often changed by what happened in between.
example: The Hobbit is subtitled “There and Back Again”: Bilbo leaves his hole at Bag End and returns to it, altered.

name: Cliffhanger
definition: Ending a chapter or episode at a moment of high suspense, so the reader has to go on.
example: Dickens’s novels came out in monthly parts, and many parts ended mid-crisis to sell the next one.

name: Red herring
definition: A false clue that leads the reader, and often the characters, away from the truth.
example: Detective stories are built on them: the suspicious butler who turns out to be innocent.

name: Chekhov’s gun
definition: The principle that every element in a story should matter: if a gun appears in the first act, it should be fired by the last.
example: Chekhov advised writers to cut a rifle on the wall if no one was ever going to fire it.

name: MacGuffin
definition: An object or goal that drives the plot because the characters want it, though what it is matters little.
example: The jewel-encrusted falcon in Dashiell Hammett’s The Maltese Falcon, which everyone chases.

name: Plot twist
definition: A sudden turn that overturns what the reader expected, ideally surprising yet, looking back, inevitable.
example: In Dickens’s Great Expectations, Pip’s secret benefactor is not the wealthy Miss Havisham, as he assumed, but the convict Magwitch.

name: Unreliable narrator
definition: A narrator whose account cannot be fully trusted, through madness, self-deception, ignorance or lies.
example: True! — nervous — very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am; but why will you say that I am mad?

name: Dramatic irony
definition: When the audience knows something a character does not, so their words and actions carry a meaning they cannot see.
example: We know Juliet is only drugged, so Romeo’s grief and suicide in the tomb are unbearable to watch.

name: Verbal irony
definition: Saying one thing while meaning something different, often the opposite.
example: Mark Antony repeats that “Brutus is an honourable man” until the phrase means its opposite.

name: Situational irony
definition: When the outcome of events is the opposite of what was intended or expected.
example: In O. Henry’s “The Gift of the Magi”, a wife sells her hair to buy her husband a watch chain, while he sells his watch to buy her combs.

name: Cosmic irony
definition: Irony in which fate, the gods or the universe seem to toy with human hopes. Also called the irony of fate.
example: Thomas Hardy’s novels often turn on it: a letter slipped under a door that slides beneath the carpet and is never read, in Tess of the d’Urbervilles.

name: Deus ex machina
definition: Latin for “god from the machine”: an unexpected, improbable event that suddenly resolves a plot.
example: In Greek drama a god was lowered by crane to settle the plot; in later fiction, a long-lost rich uncle dies at just the right moment.

name: False protagonist
definition: A character presented as the hero who is removed, often killed, partway through, shifting the story to someone else.
example: Marion Crane in Robert Bloch’s Psycho, gone before the story is half over.

name: Backstory
definition: The history of characters or setting before the story begins, revealed as needed to explain the present.
example: Miss Havisham’s jilting on her wedding day, years before Pip meets her, explains the stopped clocks and the rotting cake.

name: Exposition
definition: Information the reader needs about characters, setting and situation, given at the start or woven in as the story goes.
example: Emma Woodhouse, handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and happy disposition, seemed to unite some of the best blessings of existence

name: Subplot
definition: A secondary line of story that runs alongside the main plot, echoing, contrasting or complicating it.
example: Gloucester and his two sons in King Lear mirror Lear and his daughters.

name: Callback
definition: A later reference to an earlier line, image or moment, which gains new meaning through repetition.
example: A phrase spoken lightly in the first chapter returns at the end, now heavy with everything that has happened.

name: Point of view
definition: The position from which a story is told: first person (“I”), second (“you”), or third (“he”, “she”, “they”), limited or all-knowing.
example: Call me Ishmael (first person).

name: Stream of consciousness
definition: Writing that follows the flow of a character’s thoughts, feelings and memories as they come, often without ordinary logic or punctuation.
example: Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway drifts from the flowers Clarissa is buying to her girlhood at Bourton within a single paragraph.

name: Epiphany
definition: A sudden moment of insight in which a character, or the reader, sees something essential.
example: James Joyce built the stories of Dubliners around such moments, as at the end of “Araby”.

name: Soliloquy
definition: A speech in which a character alone on stage speaks their thoughts aloud, for the audience only.
example: Hamlet’s “To be, or not to be” is the most famous soliloquy in English.

name: Prologue
definition: An introductory section before the main story, which sets the scene or frames what follows.
example: The Chorus opens Romeo and Juliet by telling us the “star-cross’d lovers” will die.

name: Epigraph
definition: A quotation placed at the start of a book, chapter or poem, hinting at its theme.
example: Mary Shelley opens Frankenstein with Adam’s complaint from Paradise Lost: “Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me man?”

name: Anecdote
definition: A short account of a real incident, used to illustrate a point or bring an idea to life.
example: Essayists often open with one: a chance remark overheard on a train, which the essay then unfolds.

name: Vignette
definition: A brief, evocative scene or sketch that captures a moment, mood or character rather than telling a full story.
example: Many of the short pieces in Sherwood Anderson’s Winesburg, Ohio work as vignettes of a single small-town life.

name: Archetype
definition: A character, situation or image so recurrent across literature that it feels universal: the trickster, the mentor, the journey home.
example: The wise old guide who appears to the young hero, from Virgil leading Dante to Merlin advising Arthur.

name: Foil
definition: A character whose contrast with another brings out the other’s qualities.
example: Laertes, quick to avenge his father, is a foil to the hesitating Hamlet.

name: Dynamic character
definition: A character who changes in an important way over the course of the story.
example: Ebenezer Scrooge, a miser at the start of A Christmas Carol and generous by the end.

name: Static character
definition: A character who stays essentially the same throughout the story.
example: Mr Micawber in David Copperfield is forever certain that “something will turn up”.

name: Flat character
definition: A character built around a single idea or trait, easy to sum up in a sentence. E. M. Forster named the type.
example: Mrs Micawber, who will “never desert Mr Micawber”, is Forster’s own example.

name: Round character
definition: A complex character with contradictions and depth, capable of surprising the reader convincingly.
example: Elizabeth Bennet in Pride and Prejudice, whose judgement, pride and wit all turn out to be more complicated than they first seem.

name: Antihero
definition: A central character who lacks conventional heroic qualities: courage, honesty, decency.
example: Becky Sharp in Thackeray’s Vanity Fair, charming, ambitious and entirely unscrupulous.

name: Protagonist
definition: The main character of a story, whose desires and choices drive the plot.
example: Jane Eyre is the protagonist of her own story, told in her own voice.

name: Antagonist
definition: The character or force that opposes the protagonist and creates the central conflict.
example: Iago, whose schemes destroy Othello.

name: Hamartia
definition: From Aristotle: the error or flaw in a tragic hero that leads to their downfall. Often called the tragic flaw.
example: Macbeth’s ambition, which drives him from one murder to the next.

name: Hubris
definition: Excessive pride or self-confidence that defies the gods or the limits of what is human, and invites punishment.
example: Victor Frankenstein’s belief that he can create life, and his ruin when he does.

name: Catharsis
definition: From Aristotle: the release of pity and fear an audience feels at the end of a tragedy.
example: Watching Oedipus discover the truth and blind himself, the audience is purged of the dread the play has built.

name: Diction
definition: A writer’s choice of words: formal or plain, abstract or concrete, old or new. It shapes tone and character.
example: Hemingway’s short, plain words and Henry James’s long, qualified ones produce utterly different worlds.

name: Syntax
definition: The arrangement of words into sentences: their order, length and structure.
example: Short sentences hurry. Long sentences, with their clauses and qualifications and pauses, slow the reader down and let thought unfold.

name: Tone
definition: The attitude the writer takes toward the subject or the reader: ironic, tender, angry, solemn, playful.
example: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife (gently ironic).

name: Mood
definition: The emotional atmosphere a work creates in the reader.
example: The opening of Poe’s “The Fall of the House of Usher”, a “dull, dark, and soundless day”, sets a mood of dread before anything happens.

name: Colloquialism
definition: Informal, everyday language, used to make dialogue or narration sound natural.
example: You don’t know about me without you have read a book by the name of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
source: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn

name: Dialect
definition: The particular vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation of a region or group, written to give characters a real voice.
example: Joseph, the old servant in Wuthering Heights, speaks in thick Yorkshire dialect.

name: Vernacular
definition: The ordinary spoken language of a people, as opposed to a literary or learned one.
example: Dante wrote The Divine Comedy in Italian, the vernacular, rather than in Latin.

name: Cliché
definition: A phrase or idea used so often that it has lost its force. Writers avoid them, or use them knowingly.
example: “at the end of the day”, “as old as the hills”, “a dark and stormy night”.

name: Didacticism
definition: Writing that sets out to teach or give moral instruction.
example: Aesop’s fables end with their lesson stated outright: “Slow and steady wins the race.”

name: Satire
definition: Using humour, irony and exaggeration to expose and criticise folly or vice, often in politics and society.
example: Jonathan Swift’s A Modest Proposal calmly suggests the Irish poor sell their children as food.

name: Parody
definition: An imitation of a style, genre or work, exaggerated for comic or critical effect.
example: Jane Austen’s Northanger Abbey parodies the Gothic novels its heroine devours.

name: Theme
definition: A central idea or insight about life that a work explores, as opposed to its subject.
example: The subject of Frankenstein is a scientist who makes a creature; its themes include ambition, responsibility and what makes us human.
